title: Dry-run: the crawl loop and its frontier
intro: About 6 minutes. The naive loop is ten lines and is an accidental denial-of-service tool. Write it, then fix politeness and termination.

steps.title: The naive loop, and why it's hostile
steps.explain: Write it first and name the problem. A single FIFO means consecutive URLs share a host — because a big page contributes many links at once — so the fleet hammers one server. You have built a load test against someone else's site.
steps.saysOutLoud: One queue means consecutive URLs share a host, so I'd be attacking one server.

steps.title: Split the frontier in two layers
steps.explain: Priority is decided on the way in, politeness on the way out. The invariant that matters: all URLs for one host live in exactly one back queue, and one worker drains it — that is what makes per-host rate limiting possible while thousands of hosts stay in flight.

steps.title: The scheduler hands out only eligible queues
steps.explain: A worker asks for work and gets the queue whose per-host delay has elapsed. Politeness and throughput stop competing: each host is contacted gently while the fleet stays busy across everything else.
steps.saysOutLoud: Each host has its own next-eligible timestamp, so slow hosts don't block fast ones.

steps.title: robots.txt is fetched and cached per host
steps.explain: Fetch it once per host, respect its own expiry, and re-check periodically because sites change their rules. It also may specify Crawl-delay, which overrides your adaptive default. This is a hard requirement rather than a courtesy — a crawler that ignores it will get your IP range blocked.

steps.title: Normalise before you deduplicate
steps.explain: Skipping this stores the same page many times and lets session IDs mint infinite 'new' URLs. Normalisation is the cheap defence that makes the dedup filter actually work.

steps.title: A Bloom filter for the seen set
steps.explain: At a billion pages an exact set does not fit in memory. A Bloom filter gives constant space with no false negatives — and be explicit that false positives mean a small fraction of genuinely new pages are silently skipped. That is the trade, and naming it is the point.
steps.saysOutLoud: No false negatives, but about 1% of new pages get skipped. That's the trade I'm accepting.

steps.title: The corrected loop
steps.explain: Now assemble it. Note the content checksum — a page whose bytes have not changed since the last crawl can skip downstream indexing entirely, which is a large saving on re-crawls.

steps.title: Bound the traps the filter can't catch
steps.explain: Calendars with infinite 'next month' links and generated link mazes produce URLs that really are new, so the dedup filter never fires. Depth and per-host budgets are what stop one pathological domain consuming the whole crawl.

closing: If they ask about re-crawl scheduling: track observed change frequency per page and feed it back into the priority band, so a news homepage is revisited constantly and a decade-old archive page rarely.
